title: I have overcome the world (John 16:16–33)
hook: sorrow turns to joy like a woman after labor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Advocate, the one called to your side. Your line was into all truth.

"A little while." Jesus says it, and the disciples start whispering to each other across the table. A little while and you won't see me, and again a little while and you will? They want to ask him, but nobody does. It's late, he's been talking about leaving all evening, and every new sentence seems more confusing. But he notices them whispering. He knows what they want to ask. And instead of a definition, he gives them a picture, one that anyone who has been in a delivery room will recognize.
screen: `A LITTLE WHILE? WHAT DOES HE MEAN?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world." Travail is labor. Notice what the picture does. The pain isn't swapped out for something else. The same event that hurts is the event that brings the joy, the way labor turns into a baby in your arms. The prophets used this image too, for Israel waiting on God's new day. Jesus applies it to the next few days. They will weep while others rejoice. Then they'll see him again, "and your joy no man taketh from you." Then the chapter's last line, the one in today's carry: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." Two honest halves. You will have trouble: no promise that life gets easy. And then, be of good cheer. The Greek is tharseite: take courage, be brave, cheer up, the same word he says elsewhere in the Gospels to frightened people. And the reason: I have overcome. The Greek verb is nikao, to win, to conquer; you may know the related word nike, victory. And it's in a tense that speaks of something already done. He says it the night before the cross, before anything looks like winning. Christians hear in that the heart of their hope: the victory is spoken before it is seen.
screen: `THE SAME EVENT THAT HURTS BRINGS JOY.`
`NIKAO: SPOKEN BEFORE IT LOOKS LIKE WINNING.`
then, large: `BE OF GOOD CHEER; I HAVE OVERCOME THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Name one trouble you're in right now, not the whole list, just one, and say it plainly to yourself, the way Jesus does: in the world you will have this. Don't pretend it's smaller than it is; then breathe in, and on the out-breath let yourself hear the second half: take courage. If you pray, bring that trouble to God with his words, be of good cheer; if not, simply let courage sit beside the trouble.
Nikao. The Greek verb behind I have overcome: to win, to conquer, related to the word for victory, nike.
Your line: be of good cheer. The trouble is real, and so is the courage. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to John 16:33 in hard seasons, as a word of courage spoken before the worst had happened.

original.note: Greek: I have overcome, I have conquered. from nikao; in the perfect tense, something done whose result stands.

chat.says: Did Jesus promise his followers an easy life if they believed?
options: No: in the world ye shall have tribulation, but be of good cheer; I have overcome.
No: he said trouble would come, so they should hide away until it passed.
He said trouble would come only to those who doubted him that night.
chat.meaning: Two honest halves: in the world ye shall have tribulation, but be of good cheer. I have overcome, spoken the night before the cross.

travail.meaning: an old word for labor in childbirth

tribulation.meaning: trouble and hardship, which Jesus says they will have

tharseite.meaning: Greek: take courage, be brave, cheer up

nike.meaning: Greek for victory, related to nikao
